corr.head: StressTyp2's coding matches the source only in part
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Guguyimidjir; Koko Imudji: primary stress on the initial syllable; secondary stress: Trochaic (v2)". The source gives: Primary stress on the first syllable, unless the first vowel is short and the second long, in which case the first syllable is unstressed and the second stressed (magíil, gabíirr); if both first and second vowels are long, both receive equal (or near-equal) stress (búurráay). Long vowels always bear stress. — StressTyp2 (from de Zwaan 1969) codes fixed initial primary with trochaic secondary and an 'exceptional' second-syllable pattern; this matches only Haviland's no-long-vowel / long-first-vowel stratum.

sources.text: p. 41: "There is a close relationship between vowel length and stress. In a word of two syllables, in which neither vowel is long, stress ordinarily falls on the first syllable, e.g.: nambal 'stone'. A word with more than two syllables, again without long vowels, has primary stress on the first syllable, and secondary stress on all odd numbered syllables, e.g.: marrbugan 'cave', bigibigi 'pig', durrginbigu 'Indian Head (place name)'. Long vowels always bear stress." p. 42: "Long vowels in second syllables, however, complicate the stress pattern. When a disyllabic word has a short first vowel …

Weight-sensitive (vowel length): long vowels always bear stress. Disyllables: short-short = 10, short-long = 01 (primary on final), long-long = 11 (equal or near-equal stress). Longer words (long vowels only in first two syllables): initial primary plus secondary stress continuing the rhythm set by the first two syllables — SU words stress all odd-numbered syllables (bigibigi 1010), US words stress all even-numbered syllables, SS words restart odd-numbered secondaries. Domain: word in isolation (Haviland 1979:41-42).

118.dq: These stess rules apply most clearly to words pronounced in isolation; phrase stress for special emphasis occasionally alters these patterns (see section 3.2.4[a-b]).

118.heavy: long vowel ('Long vowels always bear stress'); closed syllables play no role; long vowels occur only in the first two syllables of a word
118.dflt: initial (primary) with secondary on odd-numbered syllables
118.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable, unless the first vowel is short and the second long, in which case the first syllable is unstressed and the second stressed (magíil, gabíirr); if both first and second vowels are long, both receive equal (or near-equal) stress (búurráay). Long vowels always bear stress.
118.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables, continuing the rhythm set by the first two syllables: if the second vowel is short (S-U: all-short and long-first-vowel words), on all odd-numbered syllables (márrbugàn, bígibìgi, márrbugàn-bi-gù); if V1 is short and V2 long (U-S, stress on syllable 2), on all even-numbered syllables (magíil-ngay-gù); if both are long (S-S, both stressed), restarting on odd-numbered syllables from syllable 3 (búurráay-bì-gu). Long vowels never occur after syllable 2, so non-initial stresses beyond syllable 2 are purely rhythmic.

119.srule: Secondary (weaker) stress on the accented = high-pitch syllable when it is the first or second syllable of the word; its position is set by the lexical pitch accent, not by syllable count, so it is not part of the rule string; primary stress stays on the first syllable (Glover 1969: 56-57, 60, 62; e.g. "aliq" /alí/ ['ā,lí] 'clod of earth').

However the first syllable of a foot regularly carries a slight stress <primary by comparison with the secondary stress on the accented syllable>, which serves as a characteristic feature distinguishing the foot, as a level, from the next lower, the syllable, and the next higher, the phonological phrase. ... 119.tone: Pitch accent crossed with breathiness (Glover 1969: 53-60): two emic pitch levels; 'Only one syllable of a foot may have high pitch' (the 'accent'), and 'Any syllable of a word may bear the accent, or there may be no accented syllable at all'; four tone groups on monosyllables (clear accented, clear unaccented, breathy accented, breathy low); suffixes -mae, -ba, -e take or induce the accent by rule. The accented syllable (if 1st or 2nd) carries a secondary stress; the primary word stress is initial and independent of pitch.

119.sec_rule: Weak secondary (perceptual) stress on the clear accented syllable (the lexically high-pitched syllable) when it is the 1st or 2nd syllable of the word; on syllable 2 this gives initial primary + secondary on syllable 2 ("aliq" 'clod of earth'), on syllable 1 it coincides with the primary; the accent may fall on any syllable or none, so other words carry the initial stress only. Weaker than the (already weak) initial primary, a correlate of the pitch accent, not marked in transcription; no rhythmic/alternating stresses described.
119.sec_quote: In addition, the clear accented syllable, if in first or second position in the word, appears to carry some degree of perceptual stress, accompanied by decrescendo, which reinforces the contrast between accented and unaccented syllables in the same position [...] But this 'stress' is only of secondary degree compared with the <already weak> primary stress which marks the initial syllable of a foot

tn.quote: Two emic levels of pitch are manifested in Gurung-- high, marked … in the text by "q" following the syllable nuclear vowel <and following "h" if the vowel is breathy>; and low, left unmarked in the orthographies. Pitch is contrastive on the nuclear vowel of a syllable … Only one syllable of a foot may have high pitch, phonemically, and so the term 'accent' is borrowed to refer to the high pitch … [p. 60] 3. Distribution. Any syllable of a word may bear the accent, or there may be no accented syllable at all.

morph.rootq: Hall 1953 §1.71 p.24: 'Normal, automatic on the last syllable of each word: e.g. /sòti/ 'go out' [so'ti]; /kôplotaj/ 'plot' [kõplo'taj]; etc. ... The automatic stress on the last syllable of the word is maintained in connected discourse, thus serving as a marker of word-boundaries, indicated in our phonemic transcription and in conventional spelling by a space.' (No reference to root or stem; the stress domain is the space-delimited word, which in Hall's transcription includes his hyphenated prefixes and enclitics, e.g. kabrit-la, m-ap-prâ.)
morph.elicq: §1.71 p.24 gives isolated-word transcriptions and a connected-discourse example: 'The automatic stress on the last syllable of the word is maintained in connected discourse ... e.g. /jo vini vwé mwê/ 'they came to see me' ['jo vi'ni 'vwe 'mwê].' §1.72 cites emphatic-stress forms from a named informant with date: '/se 'žoli/ 'it's pretty' ... (CS IV/6/49)'. §0.32 p.14: 'Informants, native speakers of Creole, including the numerous Haitians to whose speech I listened in casual contact in public places, and the following individuals ...'. Impressionistic field observation; no instrumental measurement and no explicit elicitation protocol stated.
morph.stmt: Hall describes Haitian Creole as having a 'greatly reduced' inflectional system that works by prefixation ('similar to that of West African languages (e.g. in use of prefixation in verb inflection and in derivation)', §0.11 p.12; 'Verbs are those forms which can take the inflectionally bound prefixes', §2.14), with postposed phrasally-bound determinant -la and enclitic pronouns on the nominal side, while 'The three processes of derivation (prefixation, suffixation, and compounding) are for the most part rare... and to a large extent only in learnèd words borrowed from standard French' (§2.3 p.34) and 'Suffixation is particularly scattering, and occurs chiefly in Gallicisms' (§2.32 p.36).

morph.elicq: Cooper & Cooper 1966:87 §0: "The language data for this paper was gathered over a period of one year, beginning in March 1963. Five months were spent living in the village of Plei Khok Honar, a 'new life' hamlet 15 kilometers west of Kontum City." No statement of how stress was observed; the paper's evidence consists of isolated citation words and minimal pairs (e.g. p.89 "pee 'three', phee 'hulled uncooked rice'"), and stress enters only as part of the definition of main vs. preliminary syllable (p.93).
morph.stmt: Halang words are 'a unit consisting of only one main syllable with or without a preceding preliminary syllable' (Cooper & Cooper 1966:93); all grammatical categories in Cooper 1965 are carried by free words — preverbs before the verb (stative jiang/ay/waʔ/jah, negative ʔbe, dependent khom/huung), free pronouns, clause-final particles — while the only affixation is derivational and prefixal (causative pə-/bə-, reciprocal tə- in the presyllable, Cooper & Cooper 1976 dictionary), plus a post-posed echo-reduplicant on verbs ('to do reluctantly', Cooper 1965 §2.1); there are no suffixes.

123.dq: Accent in Hatam cannot be stated in terms of word pattern. It is related to a whole utterance or phrasal part thereof. ... Hatam is characterised by a clear iambic metre which has full clauses or utterances as its domain, and not some kind of limited word stress.
123.quote: Notice that I formulated the stress rule for words in isolation in negative terms. Whereas suffixed pronouns and monosyllabic nouns show a trochaic pattern, bisyllabic words with or without a final clitic suggest a iambic pattern. But when these words occur in running speech, no rule can positively specify which syllable should be assigned stress. Only negatively, first syllables of polysyllabic words (whether mono- or poly morphemic) can never be stressed, suggesting a phrasal iambic metrical stress. tn.quote: Mpur clearly has phonemic tone, M eyah and Sougb a pitch-accent system. Hatam and Mansim do not have a tonal distinction, which they may well have had in the past (the number of homophones in Hatam is considerable), but Hatam does have a very pronounced iambic stress pattern over the utterance as a whole, defying attempts to determine a pattern of word stress.
tn.cite: Reesink, Ger P. 2002. The eastern Bird's Head languages compared. In Ger P. Reesink (ed.), Languages of the eastern Bird's Head, 1-44. Pacific Linguistics 524. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University.
tn.note: No tonal distinction (the author suspects tone was lost; Hatam has many homophones); prominence is a pronounced iambic rhythm over the whole utterance rather than word stress.

evidence_works.detail: A theoretical (Gradient Harmonic Grammar) account of why /a/ in an open syllable drops obligatorily before the pretonic syllable in simple nouns (pakid ~ pkidim) but only optionally in the pretonic syllable of a compound's first member (pkid mas ~ pakid mas). It treats Modern Hebrew stress as mostly final with a right-aligned quantity-insensitive iambic foot, denies secondary stress, and reports that the first member of a compound carries lesser prominence, can retract its stress to avoid clash in frequent compounds, and may lose stress altogether; no measurements are made.

evidence_works.work: Bat-El 2005, The emergence of the trochaic foot in Hebrew hypocoristics (Phonology 22(2): 115-143. doi:10.1017/S0952675705000515)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: An optimality-theoretic analysis, not a phonetic study: Hebrew word stress is quantity-insensitive and lexical, with most noun stems and all verb stems stressed on the final syllable, some nouns penultimate or antepenultimate, and nouns split into lexically stressed (immobile under suffixation) versus unstressed (mobile final) classes; proper names have unpredictable, often variable stress. In hypocoristics a binary trochaic foot emerges: templatic and -i hypocoristics are stressed on the penult and -le hypocoristics on the antepenult, with stress kept on the base name's stressed syllable.

125.prule: Primary stress (the syllable with highest pitch and greatest intensity) normally falls on the first syllable: more than 88% of the words in Vollrath's data are initial-stressed. Stress is nevertheless written phonemically because some words are stressed on the second (less often the third or fourth) syllable, with minimal pairs such as /'matano/ 'bean' vs /ma'tano/ 'must listen'.
125.srule: A predictable secondary intensity 'may be heard' in words of four or more syllables, two syllables after the primary (on the third syllable under initial stress); not written phonemically and optionally realised, so not marked in the rule string.

evidence_works.detail: Four-page SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet, 'Data checked by: Paul Vollrath (July 1992)', by the same fieldworker as the entry's source. The 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' block (p. 2) gives only three stress minimal pairs, the same three as Vollrath 1985 p. 63: mátanö 'bean' / matánö 'must listen', téle 'that distant (thing)' / telé 'scrape it!', áföle 'grave' / af´öle 'where?' (the sheet marks the stressed vowel with an acute). 'Conventions: Orthographic' (p. 3): 'Stress is written with < ´ > when it falls on a syllable other than the first syllable.' 'Conventions: Phonological' (p. 3): 'Vowels tend to be dropped in unstressed final or across word boundaries in initial syllables; especially /i/ and //.' No procedure, count or instrumental measurement is stated; the sheet's bibliography cites Vollrath 1985. Seven years after the 1985 paper the same author still treats initial stress as the unmarked default and non-initial stress as lexically marked, which is the entry's coding (kind fixed, rule initial, contrastive pairs in exc_quote). The block heading reads 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' but the block contains only the three stress pairs and no tone or length statement appears anywhere in the sheet, so tone_cls 'not-mentioned' stands.

morph.rootq: "The stress in a word in Xinaliq depends on the morphology of the word. Generally stress falls on the last vowel of the root of the word: gadá 'boy', q̇aqál 'back'. If a suffix beginning with a vowel is attached to a root ending in a vowel, it replaces the final vowel and takes the stress: ḳilí-u -> ḳilú 'friend' -> friend (DAT.); kizí-at-mä -> kizétmä 'is burning'. In derivative words, if the derivation is created by a suffix attached to the root, the stress remains on the final vowel of the root: q̇aqál -> q̇aq̇álır 'back' -> 'on the back'; dáb -> dábx̣er 'a lie' -> 'a liar'." (§3.3, pp.38-39; verified verbatim on re-open). Exceptions with initial stress are listed as probable borrowings…
morph.elicq: "It is said (Kibrik, 1994) that Xinaliq has dynamic stress. Dynamic stress is achieved through intensified muscle activity during articulation, interpreted as loudness. The stressed syllable is generally more powerful, intensive and loud in pronunciation." (§3.3 p.38). The stress section gives no statement of how stress was checked; the general methods section says only "Elicitations through questionnaires, direct elicitations, and natural speech collection techniques were incorporated during fieldwork" (§1.4 p.4), nothing specific to stress.
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing with a real prefixal component: nouns take only suffixes (13 case suffixes, plural suffixes; "It is expressed through suffixation", p.102) and in the verb "Tense and negation are signaled by independent suffixes, which have no other function, while class and number are indicated by agreement markers, which come before the conjugable parts of composite verbs. This means that the agreement markers then show up as prefixes with simple verbs and as interior affixes with composite verbs" (§7.5 p.144), with mood as "the Xinaliq verb's final suffix" (p.143); in addition "Xinaliq has an extensive system of prefixes with directional and spatial connotations... often…

morph.rootq: The morphological sources give no accent rule, only notation: 'Stress is indicated by an acute accent on the stressed syllable, e.g. wašı́ "dance". This is not part of the common Hocąk orthography ... It is, however, marked in the Hocąk lexical entries and the sample conjugated forms' (Helmbrecht & Lehmann 2006, ASSidUE 21: 10); their accented paradigms show the accent counted over the whole word including prefixes (Ø-šgáac 'he plays' vs ha-šgác 'I play', hį-šgác-wi 'we play', Table 2 p.16). The open statement of the rule is word-based, not root-based: 'One example of a rare pattern is the reported placement of pitch accent on the third mora of every word. While placing accent three moras…
morph.elicq: Hall et al. 2019: 2-3, 8, on the evidence behind the published accent descriptions: 'The data cited in phonological analyses comes primarily from three sources. Amelia Susman's 1943 dissertation, based on her fieldwork from the late 1930's, was the first to present extensive accentual data. Kenneth Miner expanded the description ... with data from his fieldwork in the 1970's ... Finally, Josephine White Eagle contributed examples from her own native knowledge of Hocank (Hale & White Eagle 1980).' 'While Hocank phonology is in many ways well-documented, there is one major gap: a lack of any published acoustic phonetic data ... impressionistic descriptions of phonetics have strongly…
morph.stmt: Hocąk verbs are prefixing for argument indexing and valency ('Pronominal marking of the arguments is - with the exception of the 3pl -ire - always prefixal', Helmbrecht 2003: 27; person prefixes 'are prefixed to the verb stem', ASSidUE 21: 7; benefactive gi-, locative ha-/ho-, instrumental, reflexive kii-/reciprocal kiki- and possessive-reflexive kara- are all prefixes), while number (-wi, 3PL -ire), tense-aspect-mood (-kjane, -nąą, -re, -šąną, -že), negation -nį and diminutive -nįk follow the stem and NPs/clauses end in enclitic determiners (=ra, =ižą); nouns themselves are almost uninflected ('no possessive pronouns..., no nominal case marking in general', Helmbrecht 2016: 430).

127.sec_rule: Helmbrecht gives an explicit alternating secondary-stress rule (every even-numbered mora after the third-mora primary), illustrated taanį́zurà 'the sugar', haakítujìkgają̀ 'after I pulled' (Table 4, p.122), while noting it is never distinctive and phonetically weak; Heiberg 1995:153 states the same ('secondary stresses fall on every other mora thereafter').
127.sec_quote: (4) Secondary Stress Rule: Words that are longer than three moras receive primary stress on the third mora and a significant weaker secondary stress on each even numbered mora thereafter. Phonetically, secondary stress is much weaker than primary stress and often difficult to identify in recordings, which may be caused by the enclitic nature of many grammatical formatives following the verb stem.

tn.quote: A stressed syllable in Winnebago has higher tone and greater loudness than surrounding syllables (Susman 1943, Miner 1979, White Eagle 1988). There are no monomoraic words (Susman 1943); bimoraic monosyllabic words are realized with a falling tone contour (Susman 1943, Hale and White Eagle 1980 (henceforth HWE)). ... Recall that high tone is a primary correlate of stress in Winnebago: the strong position of a foot is realized as high- toned. Since a DL vowel is always high-toned, it makes a poor weak member of a foot. Winnebago, then, is a prominence system.

tn.note: No lexical tone described: high pitch (with loudness) is the main cue of rule-placed stress (third mora); earlier works call it 'accent'. Epenthetic Dorsey's Law vowels are always high-pitched.

128.prule: Primary stress on the vowel of the final syllable of the stem/root (root-anchored, not word-anchored); in compounds on the last stem, with secondary stress on the first stem. Suffixes are stress-neutral and per-morpheme: inherently stressed suffixes carry secondary, inherently unstressed carry tertiary, "and there are no criteria for determining which affixes are stressed and which are not" (Shaterian 1983:64). Word-final primary stress therefore holds only for unsuffixed (prefix-only) words; suffixed words (e.g. /mhʷāli/ 'dig!', root-stressed + unstressed absolutive /-i/) have non-final primary stress. The coded invariant word-final rows (01, 001..., 00000001) drop the "(of root)" qualification.
128.srule: Stated, non-rhythmic (Shaterian 1983): affixes are lexically either inherently stressed, carrying secondary stress, or inherently unstressed (tertiary); which suffixes are stressed is unpredictable and 'must be written'. In two-stem compounds the first stem carries secondary stress (its primary reduced), primary on the last stem.
128.quote: Although the system of transcription used in this work overwrites the suprasegmentals (see 2.12), primary stress is predictable at the systematic phonemic level. It is automatically assigned to the vowel of the last syllable in the stem or root, where root and stem are the same (see Chapter Three). In compounds, primary stress is assigned to the last stem or root. If the compound consists of only two stems (with or without the addition of affixes), secondary stress is assigned to the first stem (See 2.72a-d). It is, however, not predictable on suffixes (see Chapter Three).
128.loc: sec. 2.75 'Stress Assignment', p.47. Corroborating: sec. 4.025 'Stress' p.170: 'Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the stem, and one need not write it; however, secondary stress, which occurs predictably on the first member of a compound, is wholly unpredictable on suffixes and must be written.'

tn.quote: 2.71 Pitch Yavapai has two distinctive pitch accents cooccurring with primary stress only (see 2.73). Pitch 1 is high, Pitch 2 falling (see 2.70a-v). ... 2.73 Interaction of Length, Pitch, and Stress Pitch can be distinguished only when it occurs with primary stress. With secondary and tertiary stress the pitch distinction is neutralized to a mid tone. It becomes absorbed by sentence stress and intonation. ... 2.74 Realization of Pitch 1 and Pitch 2 Pitch 1 is always realized as a high level pitch, regardless of vowel length. Pitch 2 is realized as a falling pitch.

variants.prule: In a word of two or more vowels containing a long vowel, stress usually falls on the long vowel (wherever it sits: sigma2 in vasu:k, Banya:nyuwa; sigma3 in mulvwayo:wo). No rule is stated for all-short-vowel words; the examples given (olo 'horse', thambo 'bee') carry final/second-syllable stress, and unaccented short vowels may drop (thambo ~ thmbo).
variants.quote: 2.3 Stress. In the previous sections, we did not explain which part of a word is pronounced louder or higher. When a word contains two or more vowels, we often pronounce one part louder or higher than other parts. To tell us which part is louder or higher (that is, which part of the word is stressed or accented), we can use a stress mark over the vowel--the symbol (´) for the strong and the symbol (`) for the weaker accents. For example, the word for "horse" can be written as òló. This means, then, that we pronounce the word òló with the second o louder or higher. A general rule of the accent placement is as follows: When there are two or more vowels in a word and when one of them is a long vowel, the stress is usually placed on the long vowel. Examples are presented below: vàsú:k 'to be green', jigyó:k 'to bite', wàsí:vk 'to think'. [p.40] A long vowel, then, is usually stressed, therefore in this book, the stress mark is not written on the long vowel. Whenever there is a potential confusion, however, we will write the stress mark. Some more examples are shown below: Banya:nyuwa 'Phoenix', mulvwayo:wo 'tribal office'. ... 2.4 Dropping Vowels ... When these short vowels occur in a word without being accented, they may disappear ...: thambo or sometimes thmbo "bee", nithi: or sometimes nthi: "ant" ... [p.~372] Note that when the suffix is incorporated as part of the basic form, the suffix receives secondary stress or sometimes weak stress and the glottal stop may be deleted.

morph.stmt: §1.1 p. 4: 'The language is largely agglutinating, suffixing with some fusion. Murui has no prefixes, which distinguishes it from other Witotoan languages (Fagua Rincón & Seifart, 2010; Wojtylak, 2016d).' — and §3.1.2 p. 128: 'verbal morphology is exclusively suffixing'; verb = Root + up to 17 suffix slots + enclitics (Scheme 7.1, p. 322), noun = Root + classifier(s) + number + case, enclitic =dɨ (Scheme 3.2, p. 132).

Supplemented by Minor, Eugene E. & Dorothy Hendrich de Minor. 1971 [2nd ed. 2008]. morph.rootq: Minor & Minor 1971 [2008], Apéndice II p.137: "Por regla general el acento de intensidad recae en la primera sílaba de la palabra. Cuando no es así, se marca sobre la sílaba acentuada." p.138 adds: "En casos de ambigüedad en el silabeo, se usa el signo del acento grave sobre el elemento (o elementos) no silábicos de un diptongo (o triptongo). 'caìpo' arriba." The domain is the word; Minor & Loos 1963 make no stress statement, only acute marks on non-initial stressed syllables in examples (okódɨ-kue, apéma-dɨ, hiʔdó-dɨ, uíre, haɨ́kɨ-ri).
morph.elicq: The stress rule is an orthographic note in a dictionary appendix with no statement of evidence: "Se puede leer el idioma muinanɨ más o menos según la pronunciación castellana, con algunas excepciones ... Por regla general el acento de intensidad recae en la primera sílaba de la palabra" (Vocabulario p.137). The only data statement is general: "este Vocabulario es el resultado de un profundo conocimiento del muinane" (Prólogo p.viii); the 1963 article's data "were gathered from various informants, and were checked by Ramón Zeballo Díaz, a Witoto man of about 38 years of age, who lives by the Ampiyaco River" (fn.1 p.38) and are narrative texts ('In the eight texts checked', p.47), but that…
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing in both sources: the verb "is composed of a verb root with optional and/or obligatory thematic suffixes of the century class, and obligatory terminal suffixes of one of the millenium classes" (Minor & Loos 1963 §4.1 p.48-49), noun gender/size and number markers are suffixes ("Number suffixes are of second order, i.e. they follow gender and size suffixes", p.61), and relational notions are "sufijos, agregados a sustantivos y pronombres" (Vocabulario 1971 p.133); no prefix of any kind is described. The only preposed material is free words (possessor kue/o/da, particle ape, interrogative words) and compounding fragments, none inflectional.

contra.head: Gordon (2002)'s coding depends on which source is followed
contra.detail: Three readings compete: Kerek and Hayes give secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables (the coding); Szinnyei gives secondary stress that is never final and is sensitive to syllable quantity; and modern instrumental work finds no secondary stress at all.

131.dq: In its citation form, a Hungarian word typically has a single primary stress, which falls on its initial syllable
131.heavy: None for the rule of record: Siptár & Törkenczy 2000 state initial primary stress with no reference to vowel length, codas or weight, and deny the rhythmic secondary. The only weight claim in the literature is Szinnyei 1912:12 (secondary on 3rd/5th syllable unless the 3rd is 'light', then 4th/6th), carried by Hayes 1995:330 and Blaho & Szeredi 2011:51; 'light' is not defined in the carried text (StressTyp2 guesses 'long vowels (?)' as heavy). B&S 2011:58: 'We have not found correlation between significantly high intensity and syllable weight'.

Concurring, Siptár & Törkenczy 2000:21: 'a Hungarian word typically has a single primary stress, which falls on its initial syllable, no matter whether the word is simple (e.g. »iskola) or derived (e.g. »forrósodik) or a compound…
morph.elicq: KVF 1998 sect. 3.3.2.1 p.428: 'The present description of word internal stress is based on and examples are taken from Kálmán and Nádasdy (1994). Primary stressed vowels are boldfaced.' (no statement of how stress was elicited; sect. 3.3.2.2 describes phonetic correlates -- 'Increased levels of intensity and/or pitch' -- without reporting measurements). Siptár & Törkenczy 2000:21 frame their rule for the word 'In its citation form', with sentence-level destressing treated separately, but likewise cite no elicitation procedure.
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing in inflection and derivation apart from the separable preverbal (aspectual/adverbial) prefixes: 'The syntactic and semantic functions of noun phrases are expressed primarily by suffixes (the most important of which are case endings) and by postpositions' and 'All morphological cases in Hungarian involve suffixing' (KVF 1998:191); 'Since Hungarian is an agglutinative language... There are a large number of derivational suffixes' (p.351); 'derivation proper applies suffixes exclusively... Momentary or perfective verbs are produced... by prefixing them with one or more of the several verbal prefixes available' (p.357).

evidence_works.note: Sentence-level prosody statement (p. 217, sect. 1): the first obligatory stress falls on the first content word of the comment; the verb can lose its stress and cliticize onto the element in the prominent preverbal position; an eradicating stress (sharp falling pitch accent) can fall on the preverbal element, which can only be followed by another eradicating stress on the right periphery; otherwise the rest of the sentence is deaccented or all other main stresses are reduced. The statement is the authors' own, uncited and without a stated method; the paper's own examples carry stress marks (fn. 1, p. 217: 'Main stress is indicated with (’), eradicating stress with (”)'). It says nothing about word-internal stress placement.

No acoustic data of its own; the Hungarian prosodic facts are taken from Szendrői 2003, Surányi, Ishihara & Schubö 2012 and Genzel, Ishihara & Surányi 2015.

There are three degrees of stress in Iai: primary stress, secondary stress and unstress. These three degrees of stress occur as follows: (a) Primary Stress — Primary stress always occurs on the first syllable of the word. (b) Secondary Stress — Secondary stress occurs on the final syllable of all tri-syllabic words, while it occurs on the penultimate syllable in words of more than three syllables. (c) Unstress — The syllable nuclei not covered by (a) and (b) are unstressed." Tryon 1968:2, examples ("Primary stress = [´]; secondary stress = [`]; unstress = unmarked"…

morph.rootq: "In Iai, stress is non-phonemic. It is conditioned by the syllable and nuclear structure of the word. ... (a) Primary Stress — Primary stress always occurs on the first syllable of the word. (b) Secondary Stress — Secondary stress occurs on the final syllable of all tri-syllabic words, while it occurs on the penultimate syllable in words of more than three syllables. (c) Unstress — The syllable nuclei not covered by (a) and (b) are unstressed." (Tryon 1968: 1). The rule is stated over 'the word' ('A Iai utterance containing no pauses and not more than one syllable bearing primary stress is a word', p. 1) with no mention of root, stem or affix; the p. 2 examples include possessor-suffixed…
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was observed. The only evidence presented is a list of isolated citation words: "Examples: Primary stress [´]; secondary stress [`]; unstress unmarked. Words of one syllable: /kɔ́/ whale; /lú/ girl; /bán/ his head; /ǰón/ back. Words of two syllables: /mómo/ woman; /hínat/ old man; /bárin/ his forehead; /únɛn/ skin. Words of more than two syllables: /émakàn/ eye; /máhiñɛ̀n/ uncle; /húčučè/ lightning; /bárakɔ̀ñɛn/ ear." (p. 2). Preface: "This monograph is based on linguistic material collected during fieldwork in the Loyalty Islands ... during the period May to December 1965, and in July 1966" with two named principal informants (p. iii).
morph.stmt: Tryon gives no one-line typological summary; what the grammar shows is that Iai verbs carry almost no inflectional affixes — subject person and tense live in an obligatory preverbal pronoun-tense word ("Tense is indicated only by the Pronoun used, as Iai has different sets of Pronouns for Present, Future and Past Tense", p. 46), and negation (ča), aspect (tika, θɛp) and the articles (ke, ǰe) are preposed particles — while bound morphology proper is SUFFIXAL for possession (-k/-m/-n/-tin/-m̥un/-bun/-rin, pp. 68-74) and transitivity (-ɔ/-ö, pp. 110-112), CIRCUMFIXAL (prefix + suffix) for derivation (causative/verbaliser o-…-ɔ, reciprocal ü-…-köu, nominaliser ü-…-POSS / i-…-ɛn, pp. 107-113)…

133.prule: Stress, treated as a non-phonemic intonation element, always falls on the final syllable of a word; which words are stressed depends on sentence emphasis (any word receiving emphasis is stressed). No secondary stress mentioned.
133.srule: Not mentioned in Asmah Haji Omar 1969, §2.6 'Intonation' pp. 69-70 (whole section read): one statement of final-syllable word stress inside a non-phonemic treatment of intonation, nothing on secondary or rhythmic stress. (Also silent: Adelaar 1992: 23; Anonby 2020. Richards 1981: xv describes no secondary stress, only 'even' stress on penult and final in certain schwa-penult words with a closed final syllable.)
133.quote: For the purpose of this thesis, intonation is regarded as comprising stress, pitch and vowel quantity. These three elements are not phonemic. The stress is considered as the primary intonation element, as a heavy stress is usually accompanied by a high pitch and a longer duration of the vowel which forms the nucleus of the stressed syllable. Stress in Iban always falls on the final syllable of a word. Any word receiving emphasis, with or without an emphasizing word (cf. 4.37), is stressed. At the end of a sentence, the intonation forms a contour which is either falling or rising.

morph.rootq: §2.6 Intonation, pp.69-70: 'For the purpose of this thesis, intonation is regarded as comprising stress, pitch and vowel quantity. These three elements are not phonemic. The stress is considered as the primary intonation element, as a heavy stress is usually accompanied by a high pitch and a longer duration of the vowel which forms the nucleus of the stressed syllable. Stress in Iban always falls on the final syllable of a word. Any word receiving emphasis, with or without an emphasizing word (cf. 4.37), is stressed.' (The domain named is the word; roots, prefixes and the suffix -ka are not mentioned in connection with stress anywhere in the thesis.)
morph.elicq: The stress statement (§2.6) names no evidence base; the abstract says 'Only a brief account of the various intonation types is given.' The thesis-wide data statement, §1.4 Collection of Data p.28-29: 'A tape-recorder was used to record spontaneous conversations between two or sometimes three individuals, as well as narrations by single individuals. In the home-base in Kuala Lumpur, checkings were rendered possible by the availability of native speakers there. The weekly newsletter Sarawak Karang Saminggu ... and some Iban publications ... also form sources of material for this study.' (fieldwork Sibu/Kanowit/Kapit 1964, Kuching/Betong 1966).
morph.stmt: Overwhelmingly prefixing: 'In Iban, with the exception of one suffix (Suf), all the bound morphemes are prefixes (Pre)' (§3.0 p.75); 'There are altogether eleven affixes in Iban, eight verbal and three nominal. The suffix belongs to the verbal class. One of the verbal prefixes and the suffix form a discontinuous morpheme' (§3.0 p.77); word template '(Pre) + (Pre) + (Pre) + (R) + (Pre) + R + (Suf)', 'not more than two prefixes and a suffix can occur in a stem' (p.76-77); abstract: 'The bound morphemes, comprising prefixes and one suffix'.

133.cfw: Asmah Haji Omar's grammar (1969/1981, pp. 69-70) gives final stress, but only as a non-phonemic intonation element tied to emphasis, and Scott (1957: 509) reports just 'slightly increased stress on the final syllable' for words in isolation, whereas Richards's standard dictionary (1981: xiv-xv) states an explicit word-level penultimate-unless-schwa rule, stable under affixation and with worked examples, which Adelaar (1992: 23), the leading Malayic comparativist, adopts with Asmah and Scott in hand, and Howell & Bailey (1900: viii) also accent the first syllable of disyllables; the remaining final-stress witness, Anonby (2020), describes Sebuyau rather than Iban proper in a non-phonological dissertation, so two authoritative first-hand accounts disagree on the placement of main stress and no third source settles it.

134.dq: In disyllabic words, the first syllable of a word generally receives main stress. In trisyllabic words (and longer), the first syllable is assigned main stress, but odd-numbered syllables have a secondary stress and even-numbered syllables are weak (Árnason 1985). ... In addition, contrastive focus can assign phrasal stress to nearly any part of the utterance when needed (Árnason 1985).

134.srule: In words of three or more syllables, odd-numbered syllables after the initial main stress (3rd, 5th, 7th...) carry secondary stress; even-numbered syllables are weak.
134.quote: In disyllabic words, the first syllable of a word generally receives main stress. In trisyllabic words (and longer), the first syllable is assigned main stress, but odd-numbered syllables have a secondary stress and even-numbered syllables are weak (Árnason 1985). Alternations in stress patterns can be induced by certain prefixes (e.g. ó- “un-”), and some derivational suffixes attract stress, even if they occupy an even-numbered syllable (Árnason 1987, Bergsveinsson 1963).

morph.elicq: Flego & Berkson 2020:1: "The data presented in this study are from Guðbjartur Hákonarson, a speaker from Reykjavík." The stress rule itself is cited from the literature ("(Árnason 1985)", "(Árnason 1987, Bergsveinsson 1963)"), while stress marks are transcribed on isolated example words throughout and on the recorded connected passage (p.10: "in the illustrative passage below, fara úr kápunni is realized by our informant as [ˌfaːruˈkʰauː…], avoiding a stress lapse between the two prominent syllables"). morph.stmt: Flego & Berkson 2020:11: "Icelandic is a highly inflected fusional language. To save space, its inflectional suffixes are glossed using one abbreviation each for person, plurality, tense, mood, gender, case, and definiteness"; Jonsson 1927 sec. 2: "the article is suffixed to it" -- i.e. all inflection (case/number/gender, the definite article, person/tense/mood, middle -st) is suffixal (with ablaut in strong verbs), derivation is predominantly suffixal (nominalizers -and-/-ar-/-un, verbalizer -ka, anticausative -na), and the only prefixes are a few derivational ones such as ó- 'un-' and all- 'very'.

Cochabamba: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano / Ministerio de Educación y Cultura. 644 pp. (grammar notes 'Apuntes gramaticales' pp. 9-56 with affix-order charts Cuadros I-VII; dictionary entries with translated example sentences pp. 57ff.)
morph.rootq: p.6: 'Por lo general, el acento prosódico recae en la primera sílaba de palabras bisilábicas y en la segunda de palabras polisilábicas. De otro modo, se indica el acento ortográfico. Ej.: vite "murciélago", nuyana "voy", nívape "mi pie", tijahúchava "repentinamente".' (The rule counts syllables of the whole word, prefixes included: nu-yána 'voy' has stress on the root only because the prefix is syllable 1; ní-vape 'mi pie' is an orthographically marked exception with stress on the possessor prefix.)
morph.elicq: No methodological statement accompanies the stress rule; the only relevant text is the orthographic note itself (p.6, 'Por lo general, el acento prosódico recae en la primera sílaba de palabras bisilábicas y en la segunda de palabras polisilábicas. De otro modo, se indica el acento ortográfico.') and the acknowledgment that the work rests on the authors' fieldwork with named Ignaciano speakers (Agradecimientos: 'agradecen a Dario Fabricano Ch., Marcial Jare A., Concepción Nuni de Chappy, José Anselmo Sativa, y Ricardo Tumo S. por su ayuda ... en la preparación de esta obra').
morph.stmt: Ott & Ott describe a verb with one obligatory pre-root zone (subject/possessor pronominal prefix, optionally followed by imperative -a-/-cu- and causative/attributive -imi-, -ca-, -e-, -ve-, -ma-, -si-) and a long chain of suffix slots after the root (thematic, relativizer, voice, order, object, emotive, number, mode, aspect, qualifying; Cuadros I-III, pp.12-15): 'En todos los verbos, con pocas excepciones, el sujeto está indicado por un afijo. En los verbos transitivos se indica el complemento también mediante un sufijo' (p.9); 'En el ignaciano, se puede modificar el sentido de casi todas las palabras al agregar afijos' (p.35) — i.e. predominantly suffixing, with obligatory person prefixes.

135.cfw: Ott & Ott (1959, 1967, 1983) and Carvalho & Rose (2018, drawing on Olza Zubiri et al. 2002) all put Ignaciano accent on the second syllable of longer words and the first syllable of disyllables, and the only tension is whether the few initial-accented longer words (sarare 'animal', máyusi 'pineapple') and the surface-initial accents produced by prefix-vowel elision make the system 'phonemic', as the Otts' phoneme sketch says, or a default rule with marked exceptions, as the Otts' own 1983 note and Carvalho & Rose treat it, so the placement is secure but the 'exceptionless' label is too strong.

136.cfw: Whether Indonesian has word stress at all is an open debate: Cohn & McCarthy 1994, Halim 1981 and Soderberg & Olson 2008 describe fixed penultimate stress (final after a schwa penult), while the instrumental and perception experiments of van Zanten & van Heuven 1998, Goedemans & van Zanten 2007 and van Zanten & Goedemans 2009 find no word stress in the dominant Javanese-influenced variety, only a phrasal accent on one of the last two syllables, and Farinella, Kaland & Kaufman 2025 find word-level penultimate prominence in eastern speakers but not in a Javanese speaker, so the answer depends on the speaker's substrate and the status of the standard variety is still contested.

137.dq: Nearly every Ingush simplex word has a tonic syllable, and in nearly all Ingush words the tonic syllable is the initial syllable. Phonetically, stress is marked by greater prominence and the capacity to bear phrasal accent; a word pronounced in isolation has primary phrasal accent on its stressed syllable, which is therefore higher in pitch than the rest.
137.dloc: Nichols 2011 Ingush Grammar §4.1.1 p.99; §2.1 p.16: "now stress in Ingush is almost always word-initial"; StressTyp2 entry (Nichols 1994:87) + words ˈmott ˈtassa ˈbeaccara ˈkinaška
137.prule: Stress (the tonic syllable) falls on the initial syllable of the simplex word, suffixed or not (kúotam, kúotamazhka, lóalaxuochyngara); a small listed set of words has second-syllable stress (Nichols 2011 §4.1.1).
137.srule: No secondary stress in simplex words; compounds (and adjective+noun, genitive+noun and numeral+noun phrases, parsed like compounds) have primary stress on the first element and secondary stress on the second (Nichols 2011 4.1.1-4.1.2). Not rhythmic; no marks in the rule string.

137.tone: Minimal tone system distinct from stress: a handful of grammatical morphemes (proclitics cy=, my=; suffixes -ac, -andz-, -ar, -a.d/-aa.d, -al; enclitics ='a, =ji, =j/-ii; imperfect verb roots) carry a high or rise-fall tone on the morpheme or the preceding syllable; 'Stress, phrasal accent, and tone are three separate phonemic categories' (Nichols 2011 4.2 pp. 105-106, p. 99).

tones: high (realized as high or rise-fall), vs. unmarked / lack of tone
tn.quote: Ingush prosody consists of stress, usually initial but in a few instances on the second syllable; a rule of phrasal accent ...; a minimal tone opposition (high vs. unmarked), distinct from stress; and pitch declination ... Stress, phrasal accent, and tone are three separate phonemic categories. ... In Ingush a handful of morphemes (all of them grammatical formatives) carry a tone realized as high or rise-fall on the tone-bearing morpheme or (if it is enclitic) on the preceding syllable ... Hence Ingush has both stress (mostly fixed initial) and tone (high vs. lack of tone).
tn.cite: Nichols, Johanna. 2011. Ingush Grammar (University of California Publications in Linguistics 143). Berkeley: University of California Press (eScholarship item 3nn7z6w5).
tn.locator: Ch. 4 intro p. 99; sec. 4.2 Tone p. 105 and p. 108
tn.note: Minimal privative system: one high (rise-fall) tone on about a dozen grammatical morphemes and imperfect verb roots, one per word; roots lack lexical tone; fixed initial stress is separate.

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Oto; Chiwere: primary stress on the initial syllable if it is heavy, else on the peninitial syllable if it is heavy, else on the peninitial syllable; no information on secondary stress". 138.prule: Free (contrastive) primary accent on one of the first two syllables of the word (añį́ 'he has' vs áñį 'I have'; Greer: ráwe 'beaver' vs rawé 'to count'); regular shift from first to second syllable of a disyllabic stem under vowel amalgamation in composition; prefixation can shift stress leftward (Greer).
138.srule: Two secondary accents (Whitman 1947:238 sec. 7): (i) a rhythmic, non-contrastive secondary that falls automatically on the third syllable after the syllable bearing the primary accent (unwritten in Whitman's transcription; no examples, iteration in longer words not stated); (ii) in compound words, a secondary (grave accent) on a syllable after the primary, at the second member's original primary-accent position or on a vowel produced by amalgamation at the junction (ną́-hùje 'tree stump', čí-ahàdaįñe 'little out-house', agúǰòkeñe 'moccasin'). Greer 2016:188 adds only that suffixes/infixes add a secondary stress, placement not analysed.

morph.rootq: Greer 2016 §2.3 p.188: 'Stress is both volume and pitch-based, with phonemic value in Baxoje-Jiwere, as in ráwe "beaver" and rawé "to count" ... When a root word with two syllables has additional affixes attached to it, the basic stress (and pitch) pattern can change, typically with primary stress shifting to the left in the case of prefixation, and addition of a secondary stress in the case of infixes or suffixes. An adequate prediction of stress patterns is beyond the scope of this grammar.' Whitman 1947 §7 p.238 (the statement our catalog coding rests on) is word-based: 'The Ioway language has a free primary accent on one of the first two syllables of a word. ... There is regularly a…
morph.elicq: Neither source states how stress was determined. Greer's evidence is lexical minimal pairs cited from dictionaries/field notes: 'as in ráwe "beaver" and rawé "to count" (Goodtracks n.d.), or gísa "to laugh at another (v.)" vs. gisá "a knot (n.)" (Dorsey n.d.)' (p.188); for vowel length she mentions 'a recording of a key word list by a Otoe/Jiwere speaker' (p.187) but not for stress. Whitman's data statement: 'The author's grammatical notes, vocabulary lists, and colloquial texts were obtained from Mr. Small' (p.233), with accent illustrated by isolated minimal pairs 'áñi he has, añí I have; wáñi meat, wañí he has them' (p.238).
morph.stmt: Predominantly prefixing on the verb with a smaller post-stem zone: 'the most complex morphology involves the verb, which may include basic verb stem, plus up to ten "slots" or positions for a number of possible prefixes, as well as at least four positions for potential suffixes' (Greer 2016 p.198) — person (agent/patient), locative, possessive, dative, reflexive and instrumental markers are prefixes; causative -hi, negation -skųñį, plurals -ñe/-wi, future -hñe and the mood/evidential/gender particles follow the stem; nouns take no case or number inflection and are derived from verbs chiefly by the prefix wa-.

138.sec_quote: Ioway has two types of secondary accent. The first is rhythmically determined by the position of the primary accent and falls on the third syllable after the one bearing the primary accent. ... it is ignored in our transcription. The second type of secondary accent is free in position with relation to the primary accent. ... It occurs in compound words

contra.head: Another variety (Munster Irish) is described with weight-sensitive stress
contra.detail: Munster Irish (Corca Dhuibhne, Co. Kerry; Ó Sé 2000 and Ó Sé 2008: 96 as quoted by Iosad 2013: 67) places word stress on a heavy second syllable, else on a heavy third syllable after two light ones, else on the first syllable, a system that Iosad 2013: 66 calls 'different from the quantity-insensitive left-aligned stress of other varieties of Irish' and that Green 1996: 1 describes as stress 'attracted to heavy syllables' (a long vowel or diphthong); this entry's initial rule and quoted passage (Ní Chasaide 1999: 115, a Gaoth Dobhair, Co. Donegal speaker) are those of Connacht and Ulster Irish.

ev.text: The most concise description of the basic stress pattern of Munster Irish is given by Ó Sé (2000). I quote this in the author's own translation (Ó Sé 2008:p. 96): Word stress falls on the second syllable if it is heavy, on the third syllable if it is heavy and the preceding syllables are light, and on the first syllable in all other cases.

139.dq: Primary lexical stress is located on the first syllable of most words.
139.dloc: Ní Chasaide 1999 Handbook of the IPA p.115 (archive.org); Windsor 2017
139.srule: Munster (Corca Dhuibhne) Irish, O Se 2000 as reported by Iosad 2013: secondary stress falls on heavy syllables outside the main stress, with frequency hedges: 'sometimes' on a heavy third syllable under initial main stress (H'LH` udaras), regularly when a further syllable follows (H'LH`L udaraiseach, H'LH`H utamalai); 'often' on a heavy fourth syllable under initial main stress (L'LLH` formaduil); and 'often' on the initial syllable when main stress is on the third (L`LH' ceannaitheoir; Iosad p. 93 suspects this case is postlexical boundary prominence). None in all-light words (L'LLL); reduced [@]/[I] never bear stress.
139.quote: Primary lexical stress is located on the first syllable of most words.
139.loc: p. 115, Suprasegmentals section (description based on a native speaker of Gaoth Dobhair, Co. Donegal)
139.idn: Language-level record. The rule string (initial) and the quoted passage (Ní Chasaide 1999: 115, describing a Gaoth Dobhair, Co. Donegal speaker) are the pattern of Connacht and Ulster Irish ('quantity-insensitive left-aligned stress of other varieties of Irish', Iosad 2013: 66). Munster Irish (Corca Dhuibhne; Ó Sé 2000 and Ó Sé 2008: 96 as quoted by Iosad 2013: 67) is described with weight-sensitive stress and is carried on this entry as another variety, not as a separate record; the secondary-stress statement (Ó Sé 2000 apud Iosad 2013: 70) and the listed exceptional forms (Ó Sé 2000: 48 apud Iosad 2013: 69) come from that Munster description, Iosad 2013: 69 noting that the [ə]-initial adverbs and inflected prepositions 'have non-initial stress in the majority of Irish dialects, even those with fixed initial stress'.

morph.rootq: Dillon & O Croinin 1961 p.11: 'As a general rule the stress is on the first syllable ... In West Munster, however, there are exceptions to the rule of initial stress as follows: i. If the second syllable is long, it bears the stress: cailín, garsún, tógálach, except for some verbal endings. ii. When the first two syllables are short and the third is long, the third syllable bears the stress: amadán. iii. Where the second syllable contains -ach- and there is no long syllable, the second syllable bears the stress: coileach, beannacht.' And p.67, on 2nd-conjugation future/conditional forms (imeod, osclód, d'osclóinn): 'Note that all these forms have the stress on the second syllable.' Iosad…

140.dq: The stress generally falls on the final syllable of a polysyllabic word, but there are several exceptions. Some words are accented on the first syllable, for example, rémuzd "sun," ári "work," ṹṧkəz "key," úžˊdən "millet," úrvəs "barley." Some disyllabic and trisyllabic verbs permit free placement of stress, in accordance with the rhythm of the phrase.

morph.src: Main source: Grierson, George A. 1920. Ishkashmi, Zebaki, and Yazghulami: an account of three Eranian dialects. London: Royal Asiatic Society (Prize Publication Fund V). archive.org id ishkashmizebakiy00grieuoft (public domain) -- grammar sections IV Inflexion (pp.29-57) + interlinear 'Ishkashmi Story' (pp.59-65, 38 sentences, word-by-word glosses, stress marked). SUPPLEMENTARY (stress rule + modern morphology sketch): Steblin-Kamenskij, I.M. 1998. 'EŠKĀŠ(E)MĪ', Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/6: 614-615 (archived copy (Internet Archive, 2026)).
morph.rootq: Grierson 1920 states no stress rule at all; he only transcribes it: '(An acute accent, as in wádak, indicates stress.)' (p.59, head of the Story) and 'The stress-accent, when known, is indicated by ´, as in áγad.' (p.69, Vocabulary). The rule behind our E=RIGHT coding is Steblin-Kamenskij 1998 (Iranica, Phonetics): 'The stress generally falls on the final syllable of a polysyllabic word, but there are several exceptions. Some words are accented on the first syllable, for example, rémuzd sun, ári work, ... úrvəs barley. Some disyllabic and trisyllabic verbs permit free placement of stress, in accordance with the rhythm of the phrase.' Neither source mentions root, stem or affixes in…
morph.elicq: Grierson 1920 §3 p.2-3: 'Sir Aurel Stein's new materials include a list of words and a story in Iškāšmī ... It was secured by Sir Aurel Stein ... September 7-9, 1915, from Qāzī Qadam Šāh ... the translation was simultaneously checked by a born Iškāšmī named Daulat Qadam.' Stress marks are given both in the connected story ('An acute accent, as in wádak, indicates stress', p.59) and in the word-list vocabulary ('The stress-accent, when known, is indicated by ´', p.69). The Iranica rule (Steblin-Kamenskij 1998, resting on Pakhalina 1959 / Zarubin / Sokolova) states no evidence type (unstated).
morph.stmt: Ishkashimi inflection is post-root throughout: present-tense person endings are suffixes and past/perfect person markers are movable enclitics ('in past and perfect tenses the endings are movable and can be attached to different words in the phrase, not necessarily the verbal stem' -- Iranica; Grierson §60 'they are separable, and are most commonly attached, not to the verb, but to some other word in the sentence'), nouns take suffixal acc. -i, plural -āw/-ó, possessive-adjective -na on the possessor, indefinite -(y)i and enclitic postpositions like -bā ('Case relations are expressed by means of prepositions, postpositions, and suffixes'), possession by a pronoun is a free preposed…

141.srule: Sources conflict. Volodin 1997:62 (sec. 2.1.2): trochaic accentual alternation (- v - v - v...), i.e. rhythmic accents on odd-numbered syllables after the initial main stress; no marked examples, odd-parity final syllable not addressed. Bobaljik (p.c.) in Schiering & van der Hulst 2010:523: 'There is no rhythmic/metrical alternation, but the prominence tapers off from the accented syllable towards the right edge of the word.' Both: syllables with a glottal stop (2010: or a glottalized consonant) carry extra prominence regardless of position.

morph.rootq: Volodin 1997 §2.1.2: «Просодическая организация слова в И.я. характеризуется акцентным чередованием слогов по хореическому типу (- v - v - v ...). Дополнительное акцентное усиление получают слоги с гортанной смычкой, ср. ниже. Фонологически значимые тоны и долгота для И.я. не характерны.» — a word-level trochaic alternation with no reference to root, stem or affixes. Corroborating, also without root reference: Bobaljik 1997 (ROA-208) 'As Itelmen has initial stress, these schwas all receive word stress.'
morph.elicq: Volodin 1997 §2.1.2 gives the trochaic rule with no statement of the evidence base (no mention of isolation forms, frames, texts or measurements): «Просодическая организация слова в И.я. характеризуется акцентным чередованием слогов по хореическому типу (- v - v - v ...).» The only nearby empirical framing is phonostatistical and concerns syllable types, not stress: §2.1.4 «Эмпирически выделено 32 модели слога. Закрытые слоги предпочитаются открытым (65% слогов в тексте - закрытые).»
morph.stmt: Volodin 1997 §2.5.1: «Типичная структура словоформы: (m) + R + (m). Преобладает тенденция к суффиксации: перед корнем имеется пять порядков аффиксальных морфем, после корня - 18 порядков» ('Typical word-form structure (m)+R (m). The tendency to suffixation predominates: five affix slots before the root, 18 after it'); prefixes carry subject person/mood, causative and detransitivizers, while case, number, object agreement, tense-aspect and all category-changing morphology are suffixal (§2.3.1, §2.5.2 «Все транспонирующие морфемы - суффиксы»). §2.3.0 also lists circumfixes as a third affix type (comitative к-...-л, detransitive ам-...-?л).

evidence_works.detail: The article analyses one recorded Itelmen song and finds that word edges, not stress or syllable weight, govern how words map to musical beats; it states that it is not clear Itelmen has a linguistic stress system at all and that the question has never been carefully investigated. It relays two earlier reports: Volodin 1976 perceives a plateau with glottal-stop syllables accentually stronger, and Bobaljik & Wurmbrand 2001 report amplitude peaking on the first non-prefix syllable and tapering off, which is compatible with but weaker than the catalog's fixed initial rule.

morph.src: Reid, Lawrence A. 1966. An Ivatan Syntax. PhD dissertation, University of Hawaii (= Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 2). Full PDF from UH ScholarSpace, 'd; page numbers below are Reid's page numbers.
morph.rootq: General rule is stated over the word, not the root: 'Acute accent is only used to indicate stress on other than ultimate syllables. Words without an acute accent have ultimate syllable stress.' (p.4, fn.9). But the one construction-specific stress statement refers to the verb stem: 'One further characteristic of these constructions is an additional stress on the penultimate syllable of verb stems having ultimate stress. Note Example 2 below, in which the stem tayo "hide" has penultimate stress in derived constructions only.' (p.145); cf. 'the presence of added stress on the stem' (p.148) and 'a characteristic intonation and verb stress pattern' (p.160).
morph.elicq: No method is given for the word-stress statement; it is an orthographic convention in a footnote resting on Cottle & Cottle (1958): 'Acute accent is only used to indicate stress on other than ultimate syllables. Words without an acute accent have ultimate syllable stress. The Cottles considered length to be phonemic. The orthography used in this dissertation however is based on the assumption that phonetic length is indicative of either (1) geminate consonants or vowels, or (2) a feature of stress in certain environments.' (p.4 fn.9). Data basis of the dissertation overall: one main informant plus 'a concordance of 50,000 words of Ivatan text collected by Mr. Cottle' (p.1 fn.1); the…
morph.stmt: Reid gives no typological summary, but his paradigms show a predominantly prefixing verb (voice mang-/may-/-om-/qi-/qipang-/pang-, causative pa-/pay-, stative ma-/na-, completive ni-~-in-, aptative chay-, cooperative pachi-, verbalisers pa-/ka-/CV-) with just two voice suffixes -en and -an (also in circumfixes pang-…-an, pa-…-en), while nominal categories are carried by free prenominal relation-marker particles and post-posed enclitic pronouns/particles: 'the difference in verbal affixation (qi- versus qipang-, and -an versus pang--an) establish syntagmemic contrast' (p.25); Formal Paradigm 1: 'mang_, _en, qipang_, qi_, pang_ _an, _an' (p.26).

142.cfw: Cottle & Cottle 1958, Reid 1966 and Gallego 2022 all put stress on the final syllable in the great majority of Ivatan words, but all three also record words with contrastive penultimate stress (Cottle's tiban 'look' vs tsíban 'accompany', Gallego's native talón vs Ilokano-loan tálon), so the language has a final-stress default with lexical exceptions rather than a strictly fixed final stress.

sources.text: "Phrasally-determined stress: Several languages in the Q'anjob'alan subgroup of Western Mayan have variable stress conditioned by phrasal position: stress is normally on the first syllable of the word or root, but shifts to the final syllable in phrase-final position. Phrasally-conditioned stress is well-documented for Q'anjob'al (5), and its close relatives Akatek and Popti' (Day 1973, England 2001)." 143.dq: Stress occurs obligatorily on the first syllable of most stems, on the syllable before a contour except in emphatic sentences and yes-no questions, and on a lexically determined syllable of some polysyllabic loans. (Day 1973:20)
143.dloc: the StressTyp2 entry (Day 1973, pages 20), StressTyp2 words ˈtʃeh, ˈtohol, ˈnahata, exceptional ˈescaˈlera
143.srule: No word-level secondary or rhythmic stress described: Day 1973 distinguishes only stem-initial, precontour and lexical stress, unranked. A word bears an additional stress on its last syllable when it precedes a juncture-plus-contour (phrase/utterance-final position; not in emphatic sentences or yes-no questions), on the first syllable of each further stem, and, in polysyllabic Spanish loans, on the source-language syllable alongside the stem-initial one (éscaléra).
143.quote: 1.7.2. Stress distribution. Stress occurs (1) obligatorily on the first syllable of most stems (for "stem," see 2.1), (2) on the syllable before a contour except in emphatic sentences and yes-no questions, and (3) on a lexically determined syllable of some polysyllabic loans. These are termed respectively stem-initial stress, precontour stress, and lexical stress. 1.7.2.1. Stem-initial stress. Stress occurs on the first syllable of each stem in an utterance, including monosyllabic stems, except that most particles (a stem class) are not stressed: ch'ócojtoj hin mám ≠ b'oj wúxtaján 'my father …

144.dq: Stress in Jaqaru is non-phonemic. It normally occurs on the penultimate vowel of the word and is frequently accompanied by a rise in pitch. In words of three vowels or more, a secondary stress occurs before the main stress. Hardman (1966:26).Vowel length is phonemic: c'aka 'bone' vs. c'a:ka 'chest'.

144.exq_: Stress in Jaqaru is usually penultimate, but it is antepenultimate in loans that were consonant-final and stressed on the penult in the donor language. morph.rootq: Hardman 1969 (ERIC ED036782), p.2: 'Stress, on the penultimate syllable of a word, is not phonemic in any of the languages.' (stress is located with reference to the word, not the root; the same passage notes vowel length 'in Jaqaru and Kawki is restricted to the first syllable of roots'). Birioukova 2014's phonological sketch (pp.20-21) contains no statement about stress or accent at all; it only quotes Hardman 2000:5 'Because of the consonant clusters, making syllable divisions is not useful.'
morph.elicq: Hardman 1969:2 gives the penultimate-stress statement as part of 'a brief outline of some of the salient structural features of the Jaqimara languages' with no indication of the evidence type (isolated words vs. connected speech); Birioukova 2014 has no stress description (her data: 'published works by Hardman, the digital database ... and my own fieldwork elicitations', p.34, but nothing on prosody). Hardman 1966 (the StressTyp source) could not be accessed openly.

144.sec_rule: Hardman 1966:26 (as paraphrased in StressTyp2, with its transcriptions): in words of three or more vowels a secondary stress precedes the main stress — on the first syllable in the transcribed trisyllables ˌwaːˈraha 'star', ˌmusˈčatʰa 'slowly', ˌšayˈkuta 'tired'; disyllables carry one stress; placement in words of four or more syllables not given. Revised by Cerrón-Palomino 1994:77-78 (own data): many trisyllables, mostly inflected or derived, carry a first-syllable secondary accent with lengthening of an open syllable ([a:páka], [su:rúma], [i:lkíri]), but others do not ([očíra], [alʸára], [atpána], [mačáqa], [ušúlʸa]); 'not well understood'. Hardman 2000:52 (excerpt): reduplicatives sometimes keep a secondary stress on the first member.
144.sec_quote: Stress in Jaqaru is non-phonemic. It normally occurs on the penultimate vowel of the word and is frequently accompanied by a rise in pitch. In words of three vowels or more, a secondary stress occurs before the main stress. Hardman (1966:26). [word list of the same lect:] ˈkaĉa 'mantra' | ˈmača 'to irrigate' | ˌwaːˈraha 'star' | ˌmusˈčatʰa 'slowly' | ˈira 'to carry' | ˌšayˈkuta 'tired'
